Tambaqui (Colossoma macropomum) is one of the largest scaled freshwater fish in the Amazon basin, with adults commonly exceeding one meter in total length. The maximum recorded size for this species reaches an ultimate total length of 110 centimeters [Li = 110 centimeters], a dimension that reflects its status as a dominant frugivore in seasonally flooded forests. Field surveys of spawning aggregations indicate that individuals attain sexual maturity at a total length of approximately 60 centimeters [Lp = approximately 60 centimeters], a threshold that typically corresponds to an age of several years under natural conditions. Newly hatched larvae emerge from spherical, transparent eggs measuring roughly one millimeter in diameter, and the initial wet weight at birth is an exceedingly modest 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams]. This minute starting mass, characteristic of the yolksac larval stage, necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding within the first few days of development.

Reproductive output in Colossoma macropomum is notably high, consistent with its status as a highly fecund characiform that broadcasts pelagic eggs during the rising-water season. Under controlled captive conditions maintained at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], females produce a maximum of approximately 300,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 300,000 eggs per spawning event] and typically spawn once per year [F_R_i = spawn once per year]. This substantial fecundity is achieved through a combination of large clutch sizes and frequent spawning events over the extended reproductive period. The ultimate wet weight attained by adults can reach 44000 grams [Wwi = 44000 grams], making the species one of the heaviest in the Serrasalmidae family. Such a large body mass is supported by a diet rich in fruits and seeds, which are abundant during the flood pulse, allowing for rapid somatic growth and the accumulation of lipid reserves necessary for migration and gonadal development.

The maximum lifespan documented for wild individuals of this species has been recorded at approximately 65 years [am = approximately 65 years] under the thermal regime of the central Amazon, where mean annual water temperatures hover near 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This remarkable longevity, exceptional among Neotropical characiforms, is thought to be an adaptive response to the interannual variability of floodplain productivity, allowing individuals multiple reproductive opportunities across decades. Comparative growth analyses using otolith microchemistry have confirmed ages exceeding 60 years for trophy-sized specimens captured in the lower Amazon River, corroborating the species' slow life-history pace. At the other end of the size spectrum, the tiny neonates, weighing just 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams] at hatching, embark on a protracted growth trajectory that spans several decades.

Morphometric data collected from commercial fisheries across the Amazon and Orinoco basins confirm that puberty, marked by the onset of gonadal maturation, occurs when individuals reach a fork length of 60 centimeters [Lp = 60 centimeters]. This length-based trigger for reproductive activation is consistent across populations, although the age at which it is attained can vary considerably depending on local resource availability and flooding regime. The species' ultimate length of 110 centimeters [Li = 110 centimeters] represents a ceiling rarely reached in heavily exploited populations, where most captured specimens fall below 80 centimeters. Estimates of annual reproductive output derived from captive broodstock experiments indicate that a single female can produce well over 300,000 eggs in a single spawning event [N_R_i = 300,000 eggs in a single spawning event] and spawn once per year [F_R_i = spawn once per year], translating to a maximum reproductive rate of roughly 822 eggs per day when averaged over the active spawning window.

Physiological studies of aging in serrasalmids have provided robust evidence that Colossoma macropomum can attain a maximum lifespan of 65 years [am = 65 years] in the wild, with growth models predicting an asymptotic body mass of 44000 grams [Wwi = 44000 grams] that is approached but rarely exceeded at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. The exceptionally high fecundity, with a peak output of about 300,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = about 300,000 eggs per spawning event] and one spawning per year [F_R_i = one spawning per year] under optimal thermal conditions of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], compensates for high larval and juvenile mortality in the dynamic floodplain environment. From the earliest life stage, where the wet weight at birth is merely 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], to the senescent adult pushing 65 years of age, the life history of this species exemplifies the trade-offs between early investment, somatic maintenance, and extended reproductive output characteristic of long-lived tropical freshwater teleosts.
